# *Source*.

:::{.callout-important}
## In Brief
Source maps the information environment around the one constraint Signal validated. You're answering a specific question: what does our organization know about *this problem*, and where does that knowledge live? The deliverable is a one-page Knowledge Map — a six-column table (Source, Type, Owner, Status, Pipeline, Notes) that inventories every digital system, person, and gap relevant to the constraint. Skip Source and Design becomes a guessing exercise built on assumptions nobody verified.
:::

Marina and I were on a call deciding what to do about our project coordinator. The role was costing us ~$24,000 a year. Work was falling behind. Billing was getting impacted. Signal had validated the constraint — this function was broken and it was costing us real money.

But before we could decide *what* to do about it — hire, restructure, automate — I stopped the conversation. "We need to understand what she actually does. Not what's in the job description — what she actually touches, what systems she's in, what decisions she makes that nobody else makes, and what's in her head that isn't written down anywhere."

That question changed the shape of the conversation. It stopped being about whether to replace the coordinator and started being about how information moved through her role. Every task she performed consumed information from somewhere — a project management tool, a client email, a subcontractor's status update — and produced information that went somewhere else. Mapping that flow was Source. We didn't call it that at the time. But it was the step that kept us from acting on assumptions instead of acting on reality.

Every modern company is an information company, whether it recognizes itself as one or not. Your CRM, your ERP, your shared drives, your inboxes — all of it is information used to make decisions. Source makes that information environment visible. Signal named the constraint. Source maps what the organization knows about it — and where that knowledge lives — before anyone designs against it. The diagnosis is not finished when the constraint is named. It's finished when the team can see — on a single page — every asset, every gap, and every piece of institutional knowledge that the constraint depends on.

## Diagnosis is not done until you know what you *have*.

The temptation at the end of Signal is to act. The constraint is named. The cost is quantified. The team feels the momentum and wants to move — hire someone, buy a tool, build something, anything. That instinct costs more than most teams realize.

To become a Co-Intelligent Company capable of Co-Intelligent Co-Operation requires knowing what you're working with — which records exist, which ones don't, which decisions get made by software, which ones get made by a person nobody has ever interviewed. Source produces that ground truth. Skip it and you won't get past the first design conversation, because nobody in the room will agree on what data exists, where it lives, or who holds the judgment the workflow depends on.

This is why Source belongs in Diagnose, not Execute. The diagnosis includes the information environment. Until you've mapped what you have, the constraint is a named problem without a buildable path forward. Once the map exists, it becomes a design problem — scoped, specific, and grounded in reality.

## Create a *Knowledge Map*

The deliverable of Source is a **Knowledge Map**: a structured inventory of every information source relevant to the validated constraint. It is a table — six columns (Source, Type, Owner, Status, Pipeline, Notes), one row per source — that fits on a single page. Digital systems, people, and gaps all appear as rows in the same table, because a workflow consumes all of them the same way. The Knowledge Map is not a diagram or a narrative. It is a structured reference that makes the information environment legible at a glance.

For a given Sprint and a given constraint, a good Knowledge Map fits on one page. It doesn't catalog every database in the company. It catalogs everything relevant to the constraint Signal validated, and nothing else. If the constraint is the quoting cycle, the Knowledge Map describes what is known about quoting — the pricing rules, the historical quotes, the exception handling, the customer-specific terms, the institutional memory of who decided what and why. It doesn't describe the company's HR records, its accounting close, or its marketing analytics, because those aren't in the path of the constraint. Over multiple Sprints, you'll accumulate multiple maps — and over time, those maps build into a broader picture of where your organization's knowledge lives. But each individual map stays scoped to one constraint.

The test for a good Knowledge Map is simple: could someone who wasn't in the room use this map to architect a workflow against the constraint? When Marina and I mapped what our project coordinator did, the map didn't catalog every system in the company. It cataloged what the coordinator touched, what she decided, and what would break if she disappeared tomorrow. 

{{< excalidraw ch05-knowledge-map-pm-case-study "Knowledge Map: PM Agent Team case study — six-column inventory of information sources." >}}

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
If your Source output doesn't fit on one page, it's not scoped to the constraint. You've drifted into a general data audit. Cut it back down.
:::

{{< excalidraw ch05-knowledge-map-table "Knowledge Map: six-column structure with sample rows for Digital, Organic, and Missing sources" >}}

**Building your Knowledge Map.** Start with a blank page and the constraint statement Signal produced. Draw six columns: *Source*, *Type*, *Owner*, *Status*, *Pipeline*, *Notes*. The first four columns are the Knowledge Map. The fifth — Pipeline — is the Data Pipeline Audit. Run them together, not as separate exercises. Then work through three passes.

**Pass 1 — Digital.** List every digital source that touches the constraint — the CRM records, the process logs, the shared drives, the inboxes, the spreadsheets. For each one, write the name, mark it as Digital, name the person who owns or maintains it, and mark its status: Clean (data is accurate, current, and usable as-is), Needs Work (data exists but has quality or format problems), or Missing (the data should exist but doesn't). Then answer four Pipeline Audit questions: Does this source connect to the other systems that touch the constraint, or does data move by manual export? Can a workflow read data from this source directly, or does someone have to export and re-enter it first? Who owns the handoff — a person, a scheduled job, or nobody? When was the data last verified as accurate? Mark each digital source's pipeline as *Connected*, *Manual*, or *Broken*. (If the terms "API," "MCP," and "connector" are new to you, the section "How systems talk to each other" later in this chapter defines each one in plain language. You do not need to understand the engineering to fill in this column.)

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Open the constraint statement from Signal. List every digital system that touches the constraint workflow. For each one, fill in all six columns — Source, Type, Owner, Status, Pipeline, Notes. Don't filter. If it touches the constraint, it goes on the map.
:::

**Pass 2 — Organic.** List every person whose judgment the constraint workflow depends on — meaning if they disappeared tomorrow, the work would stop or degrade. The ops lead who handles the exceptions, the account manager who knows the customer's actual tolerance, the senior engineer who hasn't written anything down. Each person is a row on the same map, marked Organic. Name them, name what they know that isn't documented anywhere, and assess whether their knowledge is at risk of leaving. Be specific — not "she knows the quoting process" but "she knows the three pricing exceptions for legacy customers that override the rate card."

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Name every person whose judgment the constraint workflow depends on. For each one, write specifically what they know that no system holds. Flag anyone who's a single point of failure.
:::

**Pass 3 — Missing.** Look at what's absent. What would a designer need to know to solve this constraint that isn't represented anywhere in the first two passes? What question would someone ask about this workflow that your current sources can't answer? What decision is currently made by gut feel that should be made by data? Add those rows as Missing sources, and note what type they *should* be — digital system, documented process, captured expertise — and what it would take to create them.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Review your map from Pass 1 and Pass 2. Write down every gap — every question a designer would ask that your current sources can't answer. Add them to the map as Missing sources.
:::

When you're done, you have a Knowledge Map — one page, one constraint, everything relevant. If a row doesn't connect to the constraint, it doesn't belong on the map.

{{< excalidraw ch05-three-pass-build "Three-pass build: Digital, Organic, and Missing passes feeding into a completed one-page Knowledge Map" >}}

## Classify what you *find*.

Not all knowledge is the same. Once the map is built, classify each source along two axes and one tier system.

**Structured vs. unstructured.** Database fields, tagged articles, CRM records, spreadsheets with defined columns — that's structured. AI can use it immediately. Emails, meeting transcripts, PDFs, Slack threads, "ask Sarah" — that's unstructured. AI needs processing before it's useful. The more structured your information is, the more useful it is to an AI workflow. If a source is unstructured but valuable, flag it — that's a Design decision about whether to structure it.

**Durable vs. ephemeral.** Brand guidelines, pricing rules, process SOPs, regulatory requirements — durable. This week's to-do list, meeting notes, brainstorm output, first-pass drafts — ephemeral. Only durable knowledge belongs on the Knowledge Map. If it won't matter in 90 days, it doesn't belong.

**AI tiers.** Think of three tiers, each consumed differently:

- **Standing context** — core facts that are always true (brand rules, product definitions, org structure). Loaded automatically. AI always has it.
- **Retrieved knowledge** — documents, articles, detailed procedures. Retrieved on demand when relevant to a query.
- **Historical record** — transcripts, meeting notes, archived decisions. Lowest priority. Flagged as historical, never treated as current truth.

For each source on your map, mark which tier it falls into. This classification directly informs Design — it determines how the AI system will access and weight each source.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
An AI workflow that treats everything as equally current is an AI workflow that will confidently cite your deprecated pricing from 2019. The tiers exist to prevent this.
:::

Run the classification while the map is fresh — it goes fast and directly informs what Design builds.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Review each source on your map. Mark whether it's structured or unstructured, durable or ephemeral, and which AI tier it belongs to — standing context, retrieved, or historical.
:::

## How systems *talk to each other*.

If you're going to map where knowledge lives, you need to understand how it moves. Three terms come up constantly in AI implementation work, and they're worth defining in plain language.

**APIs** — application programming interfaces — are how systems talk to each other. Think of a waiter taking orders between a kitchen and a table. The table (one system) sends a request. The kitchen (another system) sends back food. The waiter (the API) carries the message both directions in a format both sides understand. Your CRM has an API. Your ERP has an API. When we say a system "has an API," we mean other software can ask it questions and get structured answers back.

**MCPs** — model context protocols — are how AI connects to your tools and data. An API lets systems talk to systems. An MCP lets an AI model talk to your systems. It's the bridge that allows a language model to pull information from your CRM, read your knowledge base, or check a status in your project management tool — in real time, during a conversation or a workflow. Without MCPs, an AI model only knows what you paste into the prompt. With them, it can reach into your actual business systems.

**Connectors** are pre-built integrations between specific systems. Zapier, Make, n8n — these platforms offer thousands of connectors that link one system to another without writing code. A connector between your CRM and your project management tool means a closed deal automatically creates a project. Connectors are useful. They're also the most common thing companies buy before doing Source work, which means they've wired systems together without knowing whether those systems hold the right data in the first place.

:::{.callout-note}
## A note on terminology
Different platforms use different names for the same underlying ideas. Anthropic (Claude) calls its system integrations "MCP connectors" or just "connectors." OpenAI calls them "tools." Automation platforms call them "integrations" or "actions." The labels vary. The fundamental concept does not: something that lets one system read from or write to another.
:::

The Pipeline column on your Knowledge Map is where these terms become operational. *Connected* means an API, MCP, or connector already carries data between that source and the systems around the constraint. *Manual* means a person is carrying data that a connection could carry. *Broken* means the data doesn't move at all — it sits in one place and nobody can reach it programmatically. Design will decide what to build. Source makes the current state visible.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
You don't need to understand the engineering behind APIs, MCPs, or connectors. You need to know whether your systems talk to each other or whether a person is carrying data between them. The Pipeline column captures that answer.
:::

## People don't have *APIs*.

There are three kinds of sources. Most teams and leaders default to the first — digital — because those are the ones with names and login screens. The other two categories are less obvious and more consequential.

Digital sources are the ones an audit naturally finds — the CRM, the ERP, the file shares, the analytics warehouse, the inbox archives. They're the easiest to enumerate because they have names and URLs. They're the smallest part of the actual information environment, because most of what makes the work run is not stored in any of them.

Organic sources are people. The ops manager is the source of truth for how the quoting process runs — including the three exceptions she handles every week that have never been documented. The salesperson who has worked the top account for nine years is the source of truth for that customer's pricing tolerance. The Knowledge Map treats these people as sources in the formal sense — named, located, and described — because operationally they are. Pretending otherwise is the reason data audits produce libraries that don't match the business.

At-risk sources are the third category and the highest-stakes piece of Source work. An at-risk source is institutional knowledge that lives in one person's head and is about to leave — through a planned exit, a retirement, a role change, or a reorg. The cost of losing it is invisible until it's gone. By the time the gap shows up in the work, the person who could have filled it is no longer reachable. Source is where at-risk sources get named, prioritized, and captured before they walk out the door. For most operating companies this is the single most consequential thing Source does.

When you're building your map, ask explicitly: who on this list is a single point of failure? Which organic sources are held by one person with no backup, no documentation, and a reason they might not be here in twelve months? Name them. Mark them. That marking is what makes the at-risk category actionable — because once it's on the map, Design can decide what to do about it.

Remember the developer who walked out with everything he knew? Source provides context — to the systems, agents, and humans that need to complete their work efficiently. Preventing knowledge loss is part of that. But the primary purpose is to give Design a complete picture of what's available, so the workflow that gets built has access to the right information at the right time. If I had mapped where the knowledge lived before that developer left, the handoff would have been a step instead of a slide.

## Transcripts: the *closest thing* a person has to an API.

People don't have APIs. But you can make them transcripts — and a transcript is the highest-fidelity extraction method available.

Here's why. When you ask someone to type a summary or fill out a form, they compress. They leave out the context, the exceptions, the reasoning behind the decision. Data entry is inherently lossy, because typing is slow and people edit as they go. But when you sit someone down, ask the right questions, and record what they say, you get the full picture — the judgment, the edge cases, the "well, except when" qualifiers that make institutional knowledge actually useful.

Humans evolved a sophisticated communication system through voice over hundreds of thousands of years. Typing has existed for decades. As the cost of speech-to-text drops to effectively zero, it is cheaper in both time and information quality to talk than to type. Leverage the natural architecture.

A well-structured transcript — an ops lead walking through her exception-handling process, a salesperson explaining why specific customers get different terms, an engineer describing the estimation logic behind a quote — becomes raw material an AI can reference, retrieve, and reason against. The transcript doesn't replace the person's judgment. It makes that judgment available when the person isn't in the room.

The practical move: when your Knowledge Map flags an organic source as at-risk, the first Source action is a structured interview. Not a casual conversation. A deliberate session with specific questions: What decisions do you make that nobody else makes? Which exceptions have you handled that aren't written down? What rule of thumb do you use that you've never had to explain? The output is a transcript that feeds directly into the Knowledge Map as captured institutional knowledge.

A constraint owner, a recording, and the right questions will get you there. The transcript is the artifact. The map is where it lives.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Identify the highest-risk organic source on your Knowledge Map — the person whose knowledge is most at risk of leaving. Schedule a structured interview this week. Ask: what decisions do you make that nobody else makes? Record it. Transcribe it. Add the output to the map.
:::

### Sprint · Source at Meridian.

{{< excalidraw ch05-knowledge-map-elena "Elena's completed Knowledge Map — every source, gap, and at-risk dependency in one view." >}}

Elena Ruiz cleared her Thursday afternoon, sat down with Mark, Ty, and Dave, and asked a simple question: when an RFQ hits my inbox, what do I actually do?

Her answer took forty-five minutes. She described a process nobody else in the company had ever watched end-to-end — cross-referencing customer history, material requirements, and labor estimates simultaneously, then pulling up a file called "Customer Notes.xlsx" on her desktop to check whether the customer had negotiated terms that overrode the standard rate card. The spreadsheet had 147 rows of pricing exceptions. It had never been shared, backed up, or version-controlled.

Dave added his piece — thirty-one years of fabrication experience compressed into a gut feel for estimated hours, accurate to within 10% on standard work. But he couldn't estimate materials costs, didn't know customer-specific pricing, and had no access to the ERP's job costing history. Ty described what he saw from the sales side: he forwarded RFQs to Elena and waited. He had no visibility into where a quote stood.

The Knowledge Map that emerged from that session made the information environment visible for the first time. HubSpot CRM — Connected, but holding win/loss records with no link to quotes. JobBOSS ERP — Connected to invoicing, but nobody queried it for quoting. Customer Notes.xlsx — Broken, living on Elena's desktop with no sync. Elena herself — Organic, at-risk, the only person who could reconcile all the sources. Dave — Organic, at-risk, four years to retirement with an undocumented estimation method.

That single session produced the map that made Design possible. Without it, the team would have started building agents against assumptions about what Elena did — instead of against what she actually did and what systems she actually touched. Source is the difference between those two starting points.

## Knowledge management in an *agentic* world.

Most companies treat knowledge management as a low-priority back-office function — a shared drive somebody organizes once a year, a wiki that rots the moment the person who built it moves on. That was tolerable when humans were the only consumers of organizational knowledge, because humans are good at compensating for disorganized information. They know which documents are stale. They know who to ask.

Agents are not good at this. An agent treats every piece of information it can access as equally valid unless you tell it otherwise. In an agentic world, knowledge management requires discipline: process around what gets added, by whom, when it gets retired, how to detect when the system hallucinates against outdated information, and what the mediation plan is when it does. Source is where that discipline starts.

The old data audit approach — inventory everything, organize by category, produce a tidy library — fails because it runs without a design question. The team catalogs sales data, operations data, finance data, customer data, and produces a clean deliverable nobody can use. The data was organized for humans browsing it, not for a specific workflow consuming it.

Source inverts this. The constraint comes first. The Knowledge Map is built only against the constraint Signal validated, scoped to what the workflow will actually need to consume. One constraint, one map. The map exists to serve a design decision that's about to get made, not to satisfy a documentation goal.

Garbage in, garbage out. That phrase gets thrown around like a cliche, but it's the foundational axiom of Source work. Your company's data is a massive asset — *if* you can get it into a format AI can actually use. An agent pointed at dirty data, outdated records, or unstructured knowledge with no classification doesn't produce bad answers occasionally. It produces bad answers confidently and at scale. Source is where you confront the quality of what you have before you build anything on top of it.

I learned this the hard way inside my own company. Early on, we weren't clear about taxonomies, knowledge hygiene, or how we vectorized work — and the agents kept surfacing wrong information. Old pricing, deprecated processes, policies superseded two revisions back. We'd correct it. It would surface the same thing again. It took more iterations than I want to admit before we asked the right question: why does it keep showing old information?

The answer was simple and brutal. Everything we had ever stored was indexed together — current and expired, active and archived, no distinction. The AI had no way to know what was old. Nobody had told it otherwise. If the data was in the knowledge base, the system assumed it was meant to be there.

We saw the same pattern at a client site. They deployed an application against their internal knowledge base and it kept surfacing expired information — for the exact same reason. Current and outdated content living side by side with no process for managing which was which.

The AI was doing exactly what it was designed to do in both cases. The problem was not the AI. Nobody had done the Source work before pointing the AI at the data. This is part of what needs to get worked out in Design: how information will be consumed, classified, and retired. The downstream effects — especially for retrieval-augmented generation — are real and expensive. One emerging role worth considering is a knowledge manager: someone accountable for the quality, currency, and governance of the information your agents run on. It's a role that didn't exist five years ago. It will be standard within five more.

Source is not where data infrastructure gets built. Source names the gaps. Whether to fill them, capture the judgment, or design around the limitation is a Design decision. Confusing the two phases is how Source bloats into a year-long data project that never produces a workflow.

## The *completeness test*.

Before you call Source done, run six checks:

1. **Architect test.** Could someone who wasn't in the room look at this Knowledge Map table and know what they're designing against — what data exists, where it lives, what's missing, and what's at risk?
2. **Constraint scope test.** Every row on the map connects to the constraint. If a row doesn't, cut it.
3. **Pipeline test.** Every digital source has a pipeline status — Connected, Manual, or Broken. No blanks.
4. **At-risk test.** You explicitly asked: who on this list is a single point of failure? The answer is on the map.
5. **Gap test.** The Missing column isn't empty. If you have zero missing sources, you haven't looked hard enough.
6. **One-page test.** The map fits on one page. If it doesn't, you've drifted from the constraint.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Run the six-item completeness test against your Knowledge Map. Fix any gaps. Then put the constraint statement from Signal at the top of the page and the Knowledge Map below it. That one page is what you hand to Design.
:::

Here is Meridian's completed Knowledge Map — the artifact that session produced:

| Source | Type | Owner | Status | Pipeline | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HubSpot CRM (win/loss records, deal sizes) | Digital | Ty (Sales) | Needs Work | Manual — Ty tracks outcomes but doesn't link to quotes | Has win rates by customer and job type. Missing: quote amounts on lost bids. |
| JobBOSS ERP (job costing history, 800+ jobs) | Digital | Finance / ERP admin | Clean | Manual — Elena queries by memory, not systematically | Best source for historical pricing. Structured and queryable, but nobody uses it for quoting. |
| "Customer Notes.xlsx" (pricing exceptions) | Digital | Elena (VP Ops) | Needs Work | Broken — lives on Elena's desktop, no backup, no version control | 147 customer-specific pricing rules. Mix of simple discounts and complex terms. Never validated against current contracts. |
| Elena — pricing exceptions, customer history, quoting judgment | Organic | Elena (VP Ops) | — | — | Holds the complete picture for every quote. Only person who can reconcile all sources. **AT RISK: single point of failure. No backup, no documentation.** |
| Dave — fabrication hour estimation | Organic | Dave (Sr Design Eng, 31 yrs) | — | — | Estimates accurate to ~10% on standard work. Has never documented his estimation method. **AT RISK: 4 years to retirement.** |
| Historical quote-to-actual accuracy | Missing | Nobody | Missing | — | Would validate whether rapid estimates are reliable. Data exists in ERP (actuals) and Elena's files (quotes) but has never been compared. |
| Customer segment profitability | Missing | Nobody | Missing | — | Would enable prioritized quoting — fast-track high-margin segments. Requires joining CRM win/loss to ERP job costing. |

Look at what this map makes visible. Two organic sources are flagged at risk — Elena as a single point of failure, Dave with four years to retirement. A critical spreadsheet with 147 pricing rules lives on one person's desktop with no sync. The CRM and ERP hold the data you'd need to build a quoting workflow, but nobody has ever joined them. Two pieces of information that don't exist yet — historical accuracy and segment profitability — are the exact inputs the team would need to decide whether an agent-assisted quoting workflow is viable. Every one of those findings came from working the three passes against a single constraint. None of them would surface in a general data audit.

## Hand off to *Design*.

At the end of Source, you have two things on one sheet of paper: the constraint Signal validated, and the Knowledge Map that describes the information environment around it — assets, flow, and gaps together. That is the input Design needs. Constraint plus map.

{{< excalidraw ch05-source-to-design-handoff "Source-to-Design handoff: constraint statement above, Knowledge Map below" >}}

With those two things in hand, the team moves into Design — the phase where ownership decisions get made, where the Hybrid Accountability Chart entry for this sprint gets built, and where the work crosses from Diagnose into Execute. Source is the bridge. It's the last thing you do before you're start to design your system.

## Reflection Questions

1. Build a first-pass Knowledge Map for your top constraint right now. List the digital sources that touch that workflow. How many of them are Connected vs. Manual vs. Broken in the Pipeline column? What does that ratio tell you about the design work ahead?
2. Who on your Knowledge Map is an organic source — someone whose judgment the constraint workflow depends on? Is that person a single point of failure? If they left tomorrow, what would break first?
3. The chapter describes the developer who walked out with everything he knew. Is there someone in your company right now whose departure would create the same chute? Have you scheduled a structured interview to extract what they know before they go?
4. When you classify the sources on your map, what share of your information is structured vs. unstructured? What is the most valuable piece of unstructured knowledge in the constraint workflow — and what would it take to make it AI-usable?
